SEC football, 2021–2025

The SEC

Sixteen current SEC programs, 1,040 team-games over five seasons, every one with an expected margin. Texas and Oklahoma's Big 12 seasons are included so each program has the same window.

39-24Texas A&M won-lost
+2.7expected minus deserved wins, 6 of 16
-1.0won minus deserved wins, 13 of 16
-10talent rank minus SP+ rank, 9 of 16

Every season that goes differently than expected comes down to one of three things: the expectations were wrong, the bounces were wrong, or the development was wrong. This page asks those three questions of all sixteen programs at once, then asks whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each chart ends with a short takeaway, with a note on how much to trust it; five seasons is only about 63 games per team. Every team also has its own page in the menu above.

Terms used on this page
Expected margin
How many points the team was expected to win or lose by, according to the point spread the sportsbooks posted just before kickoff. It sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public expected, with money behind it, so this page uses it as the measure of expectations. A week-earlier version (the opening number) also exists; when the two differ, opinion moved during the week.
Expected wins
Each game's expected margin converted to a chance of winning, then added up. The record the public thought was coming.
Deserved wins
Each game's postgame win probability, from CollegeFootballData's play-by-play model, added up. How many games a team that played that way usually wins. The gap between actual and deserved wins is what most people call luck.
SP+
Bill Connelly's efficiency rating of how well a team actually played, adjusted for opponent. Used here as the measure of quality, separate from the record.
Talent composite
247Sports' rating of the whole roster's recruiting pedigree. Used here as the measure of what the players were supposed to be.
Beat expectations (by)
Won by more than the expected margin, or lost by less. "Beat by" is the actual margin minus the expected margin: +7 means seven points better than expected. A bettor would say the team covered.
One-score game
Decided by eight points or fewer.
Standard error
The size of gap that random variation alone produces about a third of the time. A number within one standard error is noise. Beyond two, it is probably real. Each takeaway has a "How sure is this?" note that says which.

Overrated, underrated, lucky, unlucky

Up and down is what the public expected minus what the play deserved: up is overrated. Left and right is actual wins minus deserved wins: right is overperforming, usually close games and turnover luck. Five-season totals. A team can be overrated and unlucky at the same time; that is the top-left corner.

Takeaway: By this measure Florida is the most overrated program in the league (+4.1 wins) and South Carolina the most underrated (-3.4). Georgia has won the most beyond what its play deserved (+5.4) and Auburn the least (-5.5). Texas A&M sits at +2.7 on the expectation axis and -1.0 on the luck axis: overrated and neither lucky nor unlucky. The league as a whole clusters near the middle; the corners are a handful of programs.

How sure is this?

One standard error is about ±2.5 wins up and down and ±2.3 left and right. Beyond two standard errors on either axis: Arkansas, Auburn, Georgia. Between one and two: Alabama, Florida, LSU, Mississippi State, Missouri, Oklahoma, Ole Miss, South Carolina, Texas A&M. Everyone else is inside the noise, and the luck axis in particular needs far more than five seasons to say much.

Beat expectations by, on average

Positive means the program beat its expected margin on average; negative means the public was consistently too optimistic about it.

Takeaway: Over five seasons there is no SEC team whose expected margins are reliably off. The most optimistic the public has been about any program is 2.7 points a game (Florida), the most pessimistic 2.8 (South Carolina), and the whole league spans about 3 points. That is what you would expect when the number is set by people with money on it.

How sure is this?

With about 63 games per team, one standard error on a beat-expectations rate is roughly ±6 points. Outside two standard errors: no team.

Filled dot is the rate of beating expectations when the team was expected to win, open circle when it was expected to lose. A team far to the left on the filled dot but to the right on the open one is a program the public overbuys when it is supposed to win.

Data: CollegeFootballData.com games and lines endpoints, kickoff point spread from consensus or DraftKings where available. Expected margins are from the listed team's side. Beat by = actual margin minus expected margin. Conference games appear once for each side, so the league-wide beat-by average nets to roughly zero by construction; per-team numbers are unaffected. Expected wins convert each expected margin to a win probability with a normal model (standard deviation 14.9 points, fitted to this data) and sum them. Deserved wins sum CFBD's postgame win probability per game; where CFBD has no play-by-play for a game (0 of 1040), the expected-margin probability stands in. Talent composite, recruiting ranks, SP+, and AP polls are CFBD's season tables.

Over five seasons Alabama has been about what everyone expected: 56 wins against 55.5 expected. That does not mean nothing is going on underneath. Were the expectations right for the right reasons? Did the bounces even out? Did the roster play to its recruiting rankings? The sections below take those one at a time, then ask whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each ends with a short takeaway; a note under it says how much to trust the number, because five seasons is only about 63 games.

Expected margin

It sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public expected, with money behind it, so this page uses it as the measure of expectations. 1. Were the expectations wrong?

Every game carries an expected margin, the point spread posted just before kickoff, which sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public thought would happen. Convert each one to a chance of winning and add them up, and you get the record the public expected. Deserved wins come from the other direction: after each game, a play-by-play model estimates how often a team that played that way wins it. If the public expected more wins than the play deserved, the expectations were too optimistic.

WonPublic expectedPlay deserved
SeasonRecordExpectedDeservedWon vs expectedWon vs deservedExpected to winExpected to lose

202211-211.6-1.410.6-2.4-0.6+0.411-20-0
202312-210.3-3.711.4-2.6+1.7+0.611-11-1

Takeaway: The public kept expecting more of Alabama than the play delivered: 55.5 wins expected against 51.8 deserved over five seasons. The widest gap was 2024, 10.6 expected against 8.6 deserved. On this evidence the expectations were too optimistic.

How sure is this?

One standard error on this gap is about ±2.6 wins over 70 games, so +3.7 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.4 standard errors).

One standard error on luck is about ±2.3 wins over five seasons, so +4.2 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.9 standard errors). Luck needs far more than 63 games to measure; anything under about 5 wins here cannot be told from nothing.

3. Was it the roster?

Three national rankings side by side: the roster's recruiting pedigree (247Sports talent composite), how well the team actually played (SP+), and where the preseason AP poll had it. Lower is better. When the play line sits below the talent line, the roster gave less than its rankings promised. Above it, more.

Talent compositeSP+ (quality of play)Preseason AP (blank = unranked)
SeasonTalentRecruiting classPreseason APSP+OffenseDefenseRecord
202111134913-2
2022121481211-2
2023114711812-2
20241254689-4
202523820361111-4

Takeaway: The roster ranked No. 1 on average and the play ranked No. 8, a gap of 6 spots, and the play ranked below the roster in 5 of 5 seasons. 2025 was the low point: a No. 2 roster that played like No. 20. The offense averaged No. 13 and the defense No. 10, so the offense has been the larger drag. The comparison that matters is the league: the average SEC gap is -11 spots, because the talent composite rates SEC rosters higher than they play, so against that baseline Alabama is typical of the conference. The absolute gap is real; the relative one is not.

How sure is this?

Five seasons of rank averages carry roughly ±5 spots of noise; single-season gaps of 20 or more spots are well outside it. The league comparison is the fair one, since the talent composite is generous to every SEC roster.

4. Does it change as the season goes on?

Each faint line is one season, game by game: how many points Alabama beat expectations by, or fell short. The heavy line is the five-season average for that game of the year. The table pools the five seasons into early, middle, and late stretches. The expected margin already moves week to week as opinion changes, so a pattern here says the public was slow to adjust, in one direction or the other.

Part of seasonGamesWon-lostExpected winsAvg marginBeat by, avgPlay vs expected, per game
Early (games 1-4)2018-217.4+28.1+2.5-8%
Middle (5-8)2016-416.2+12.3-2.3-4%
Late (9 on)3022-821.9+12.1-2.4-5%

Takeaway: By margin, Alabama has faded as seasons go on: 2.4 points a game short of expectations from game 9 on, versus 2.5 points a game ahead of expectations in the first four. Because the expected margin already adjusts week by week, that means the public kept believing longer than the play warranted. In wins: 18-2 early against 17.4 expected (+0.6), 22-8 late against 21.9 expected (+0.1).

How sure is this?

One standard error on the early-versus-late margin difference is about ±4.3 points a game (20 early games, 30 late), so -4.9 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.1 standard errors). On the wins comparison one standard error is about ±2.5 wins, so -0.5 is within the noise (0.2 standard errors). Single-game swings of 20 points are routine, which is why the faint season lines look so jagged.

Bottom line: Expectations for Alabama have probably run too high (+3.7 wins, suggestive but not conclusive). It has probably been lucky (+4.2 wins, suggestive but not conclusive). The roster-to-play gap (-6 spots) is the SEC norm (-11); the talent rankings flatter the whole league, not just Alabama.

How sure is this?

The rate is suggestive but not conclusive (1.1 standard errors) against an even split; one standard error is about ±6 points at this sample size. The splits above are smaller samples still and should be treated as anecdotes.

Arkansas has spent five seasons short of expectations: 29 wins against 33.7 expected. Every disappointing season comes down to one of three things. The expectations were wrong: the team was never as good as the polls, the public, and the fans believed. The bounces were wrong: the team played well enough to win and didn't. The development was wrong: the players were there and the play wasn't. The sections below take those one at a time, then ask whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each ends with a short takeaway; a note under it says how much to trust the number, because five seasons is only about 63 games.

20233222–5456664-8
20242631–2440337-6
20252332–5316992-10

Takeaway: The roster ranked No. 27 on average and the play ranked No. 36, a gap of 9 spots, and the play ranked below the roster in 3 of 5 seasons. 2025 was the low point: a No. 23 roster that played like No. 53. The offense averaged No. 32 and the defense No. 58, so the defense has been the larger drag. The comparison that matters is the league: the average SEC gap is -11 spots, because the talent composite rates SEC rosters higher than they play, so against that baseline Arkansas is typical of the conference. The absolute gap is real; the relative one is not.

How sure is this?

Five seasons of rank averages carry roughly ±5 spots of noise; single-season gaps of 20 or more spots are well outside it. The league comparison is the fair one, since the talent composite is generous to every SEC roster.

4. Does it change as the season goes on?

Each faint line is one season, game by game: how many points Arkansas beat expectations by, or fell short. The heavy line is the five-season average for that game of the year. The table pools the five seasons into early, middle, and late stretches. The expected margin already moves week to week as opinion changes, so a pattern here says the public was slow to adjust, in one direction or the other.

Part of seasonGamesWon-lostExpected winsAvg marginBeat by, avgPlay vs expected, per game

Middle (5-8)205-158.0-5.0-2.2-6%
Late (9 on)2310-1311.8-2.3-3.5-1%

Takeaway: By margin, Arkansas has faded as seasons go on: 3.5 points a game short of expectations from game 9 on, versus 2.7 points a game ahead of expectations in the first four. Because the expected margin already adjusts week by week, that means the public kept believing longer than the play warranted. In wins: 14-6 early against 13.9 expected (+0.1), 10-13 late against 11.8 expected (-1.8).

How sure is this?

One standard error on the early-versus-late margin difference is about ±4.6 points a game (20 early games, 23 late), so -6.2 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.4 standard errors). On the wins comparison one standard error is about ±2.7 wins, so -1.9 is within the noise (0.7 standard errors). Single-game swings of 20 points are routine, which is why the faint season lines look so jagged.

Bottom line: Expectations for Arkansas have been about right (-0.5 wins, within the noise). It has clearly been unlucky (-5.2 wins, unlikely to be noise). The roster-to-play gap (-9 spots) is the SEC norm (-11); the talent rankings flatter the whole league, not just Arkansas.

Auburn

Auburn has spent five seasons short of expectations: 27 wins against 33.6 expected. Every disappointing season comes down to one of three things. The expectations were wrong: the team was never as good as the polls, the public, and the fans believed. The bounces were wrong: the team played well enough to win and didn't. The development was wrong: the players were there and the play wasn't. The sections below take those one at a time, then ask whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each ends with a short takeaway; a note under it says how much to trust the number, because five seasons is only about 63 games.

Terms used on this page
Expected margin
How many points the team was expected to win or lose by, according to the point spread the sportsbooks posted just before kickoff. It sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public expected, with money behind it, so this page uses it as the measure of expectations. A week-earlier version (the opening number) also exists; when the two differ, opinion moved during the week.
Expected wins
Each game's expected margin converted to a chance of winning, then added up. The record the public thought was coming.
Deserved wins
Each game's postgame win probability, from CollegeFootballData's play-by-play model, added up. How many games a team that played that way usually wins. The gap between actual and deserved wins is what most people call luck.
SP+
Bill Connelly's efficiency rating of how well a team actually played, adjusted for opponent. Used here as the measure of quality, separate from the record.
Talent composite
247Sports' rating of the whole roster's recruiting pedigree. Used here as the measure of what the players were supposed to be.
Beat expectations (by)
Won by more than the expected margin, or lost by less. "Beat by" is the actual margin minus the expected margin: +7 means seven points better than expected. A bettor would say the team covered.
One-score game
Decided by eight points or fewer.
Standard error
The size of gap that random variation alone produces about a third of the time. A number within one standard error is noise. Beyond two, it is probably real. Each takeaway has a "How sure is this?" note that says which.

1. Were the expectations wrong?

Every game carries an expected margin, the point spread posted just before kickoff, which sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public thought would happen. Convert each one to a chance of winning and add them up, and you get the record the public expected. Deserved wins come from the other direction: after each game, a play-by-play model estimates how often a team that played that way wins it. If the public expected more wins than the play deserved, the expectations were too optimistic.

Takeaway: By margin, Georgia has finished seasons better than it started them: 2.5 points a game ahead of expectations from game 9 on, versus 2.0 points a game short of expectations in the first four. How sure is this?

One standard error on the early-versus-late margin difference is about ±4.3 points a game (20 early games, 32 late), so +4.5 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.1 standard errors). Bottom line: Expectations for Georgia have been about right (-0.3 wins, within the noise). It has clearly been lucky (+5.4 wins, unlikely to be noise). The roster has outplayed its rankings by SEC standards (-1 spots against a league average of -11).

Over five seasons Kentucky has been about what everyone expected: 33 wins against 34.3 expected. That does not mean nothing is going on underneath. Were the expectations right for the right reasons? Did the bounces even out? Did the roster play to its recruiting rankings? The sections below take those one at a time, then ask whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each ends with a short takeaway; a note under it says how much to trust the number, because five seasons is only about 63 games.

Terms used on this page
Expected margin
How many points the team was expected to win or lose by, according to the point spread the sportsbooks posted just before kickoff. It sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public expected, with money behind it, so this page uses it as the measure of expectations. A week-earlier version (the opening number) also exists; when the two differ, opinion moved during the week.
Expected wins
Each game's expected margin converted to a chance of winning, then added up. The record the public thought was coming.
Deserved wins
Each game's postgame win probability, from CollegeFootballData's play-by-play model, added up. How many games a team that played that way usually wins. The gap between actual and deserved wins is what most people call luck.
SP+
Bill Connelly's efficiency rating of how well a team actually played, adjusted for opponent. Used here as the measure of quality, separate from the record.
Talent composite
247Sports' rating of the whole roster's recruiting pedigree. Used here as the measure of what the players were supposed to be.
Beat expectations (by)
Won by more than the expected margin, or lost by less. "Beat by" is the actual margin minus the expected margin: +7 means seven points better than expected. A bettor would say the team covered.
One-score game
Decided by eight points or fewer.
Standard error
The size of gap that random variation alone produces about a third of the time. A number within one standard error is noise. Beyond two, it is probably real. Each takeaway has a "How sure is this?" note that says which.

1. Were the expectations wrong?

Every game carries an expected margin, the point spread posted just before kickoff, which sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public thought would happen. Convert each one to a chance of winning and add them up, and you get the record the public expected. Deserved wins come from the other direction: after each game, a play-by-play model estimates how often a team that played that way wins it. If the public expected more wins than the play deserved, the expectations were too optimistic.

Every game carries an expected margin, the point spread posted just before kickoff, which sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public thought would happen. Convert each one to a chance of winning and add them up, and you get the record the public expected. Deserved wins come from the other direction: after each game, a play-by-play model estimates how often a team that played that way wins it. If the public expected more wins than the play deserved, the expectations were too optimistic.

WonPublic expectedPlay deserved
SeasonRecordExpectedDeservedWon vs expectedWon vs deservedExpected to winExpected to lose
20217-67.4-5.67.9-5.1-0.4-0.94-33-3
20229-48.2-4.87.3-5.7+0.8+1.78-21-2
20235-75.6-6.45.0-7.0-0.6+0.04-01-7
20242-104.1-7.92.6-9.4-2.1-0.62-10-9
20255-85.9-7.15.2-7.8-0.9-0.23-12-7

Takeaway: The public kept expecting more of Mississippi State than the play delivered: 31.1 wins expected against 28.0 deserved over five seasons. The widest gap was 2024, 4.1 expected against 2.6 deserved. On this evidence the expectations were too optimistic.

How sure is this?

One standard error on this gap is about ±2.5 wins over 63 games, so +3.2 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.3 standard errors).

2. Was it luck?

Luck is the gap between what the play deserved and what actually happened: close games, turnovers, and the afternoons that defied the odds. The games below are ranked by the pre-game chance of winning implied by the expected margin.

One standard error on luck is about ±2.2 wins over five seasons, so +0.0 is within the noise (0.0 standard errors). Luck needs far more than 63 games to measure; anything under about 4 wins here cannot be told from nothing.

3. Was it the roster?

Three national rankings side by side: the roster's recruiting pedigree (247Sports talent composite), how well the team actually played (SP+), and where the preseason AP poll had it. Lower is better. When the play line sits below the talent line, the roster gave less than its rankings promised. Above it, more.

Takeaway: The roster ranked No. 29 on average and the play ranked No. 52, a gap of 23 spots, and the play ranked below the roster in 4 of 5 seasons. 2024 was the low point: a No. 34 roster that played like No. 88. The offense averaged No. 52 and the defense No. 59, so the defense has been the larger drag. The comparison that matters is the league: the average SEC gap is -11 spots, because the talent composite rates SEC rosters higher than they play, so even by SEC standards the roster has underdelivered.

How sure is this?

Five seasons of rank averages carry roughly ±5 spots of noise; single-season gaps of 20 or more spots are well outside it. The league comparison is the fair one, since the talent composite is generous to every SEC roster.

4. Does it change as the season goes on?

Each faint line is one season, game by game: how many points Mississippi State beat expectations by, or fell short. The heavy line is the five-season average for that game of the year. The table pools the five seasons into early, middle, and late stretches. The expected margin already moves week to week as opinion changes, so a pattern here says the public was slow to adjust, in one direction or the other.

Part of seasonGamesWon-lostExpected winsAvg marginBeat by, avgPlay vs expected, per game

Middle (5-8)207-137.0-5.5+2.4+4%
Late (9 on)239-1410.6-4.1-3.8-13%

Takeaway: By margin, Mississippi State has faded as seasons go on: 3.8 points a game short of expectations from game 9 on, versus 0.5 points a game short of expectations in the first four. Because the expected margin already adjusts week by week, that means the public kept believing longer than the play warranted. In wins: 12-8 early against 13.5 expected (-1.5), 9-14 late against 10.6 expected (-1.6).

How sure is this?

One standard error on the early-versus-late margin difference is about ±4.6 points a game (20 early games, 23 late), so -3.3 is within the noise (0.7 standard errors). On the wins comparison one standard error is about ±2.6 wins, so -0.1 is within the noise (0.0 standard errors). Single-game swings of 20 points are routine, which is why the faint season lines look so jagged.

Bottom line: Expectations for Mississippi State have probably run too high (+3.2 wins, suggestive but not conclusive). Luck has been a non-factor (+0.0 wins, within the noise). The roster has underdelivered even by SEC standards (-23 spots against a league average of -11).

Missouri

Every game over five seasons, from the Missouri side of the expectations.

41-24won-lost, 65 games
37.3wins the public expected
38.3wins the play deserved
No. 28roster by talent, avg national rank
No. 33quality of play (SP+), avg national rank

Missouri has spent five seasons beating expectations: 41 wins against 37.3 expected. The question is how. Were the expectations too low, with the public slow to believe in a good team? Did the bounces go its way, winning games the play did not quite earn? Or did the roster outplay its recruiting rankings? The sections below take those one at a time, then ask whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each ends with a short takeaway; a note under it says how much to trust the number, because five seasons is only about 63 games.

Terms used on this page
Expected margin
How many points the team was expected to win or lose by, according to the point spread the sportsbooks posted just before kickoff. It sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public expected, with money behind it, so this page uses it as the measure of expectations. A week-earlier version (the opening number) also exists; when the two differ, opinion moved during the week.
Expected wins
Each game's expected margin converted to a chance of winning, then added up. The record the public thought was coming.
Deserved wins
Each game's postgame win probability, from CollegeFootballData's play-by-play model, added up. How many games a team that played that way usually wins. The gap between actual and deserved wins is what most people call luck.
SP+
Bill Connelly's efficiency rating of how well a team actually played, adjusted for opponent. Used here as the measure of quality, separate from the record.
Talent composite
247Sports' rating of the whole roster's recruiting pedigree. Used here as the measure of what the players were supposed to be.
Beat expectations (by)
Won by more than the expected margin, or lost by less. "Beat by" is the actual margin minus the expected margin: +7 means seven points better than expected. A bettor would say the team covered.
One-score game
Decided by eight points or fewer.
Standard error
The size of gap that random variation alone produces about a third of the time. A number within one standard error is noise. Beyond two, it is probably real. Each takeaway has a "How sure is this?" note that says which.

Ole Miss has spent five seasons beating expectations: 52 wins against 46.9 expected. The question is how. Were the expectations too low, with the public slow to believe in a good team? Did the bounces go its way, winning games the play did not quite earn? Or did the roster outplay its recruiting rankings? The sections below take those one at a time, then ask whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each ends with a short takeaway; a note under it says how much to trust the number, because five seasons is only about 63 games.

Terms used on this page
Expected margin
How many points the team was expected to win or lose by, according to the point spread the sportsbooks posted just before kickoff. It sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public expected, with money behind it, so this page uses it as the measure of expectations. A week-earlier version (the opening number) also exists; when the two differ, opinion moved during the week.
Expected wins
Each game's expected margin converted to a chance of winning, then added up. The record the public thought was coming.
Deserved wins
Each game's postgame win probability, from CollegeFootballData's play-by-play model, added up. How many games a team that played that way usually wins. The gap between actual and deserved wins is what most people call luck.
SP+
Bill Connelly's efficiency rating of how well a team actually played, adjusted for opponent. Used here as the measure of quality, separate from the record.
Talent composite
247Sports' rating of the whole roster's recruiting pedigree. Used here as the measure of what the players were supposed to be.
Beat expectations (by)
Won by more than the expected margin, or lost by less. "Beat by" is the actual margin minus the expected margin: +7 means seven points better than expected. A bettor would say the team covered.
One-score game
Decided by eight points or fewer.
Standard error
The size of gap that random variation alone produces about a third of the time. A number within one standard error is noise. Beyond two, it is probably real. Each takeaway has a "How sure is this?" note that says which.

1. Were the expectations wrong?

Every game carries an expected margin, the point spread posted just before kickoff, which sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public thought would happen. Convert each one to a chance of winning and add them up, and you get the record the public expected. Deserved wins come from the other direction: after each game, a play-by-play model estimates how often a team that played that way wins it. If the public expected more wins than the play deserved, the expectations were too optimistic.

WonPublic expectedPlay deserved
SeasonRecordExpectedDeservedWon vs expectedWon vs deservedExpected to winExpected to lose
202110-38.1-4.99.0-4.0+1.9+1.08-12-2
20228-59.1-3.98.1-4.9-1.1-0.18-30-1
202311-28.7-4.39.7-3.3+2.3+1.39-02-2
202410-310.8-2.211.4-1.6-0.8-1.49-31-0
202513-210.2-4.811.4-3.6+2.8+1.611-02-2

Takeaway: The public kept expecting less of Ole Miss than the play delivered: 46.9 wins expected against 49.6 deserved. The widest gap was 2025, 11.4 deserved against 10.2 expected. The expectations were too pessimistic.

How sure is this?

One standard error on this gap is about ±2.6 wins over 67 games, so -2.7 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.1 standard errors).

2. Was it luck?

Luck is the gap between what the play deserved and what actually happened: close games, turnovers, and the afternoons that defied the odds. The games below are ranked by the pre-game chance of winning implied by the expected margin.

Takeaway: The bounces have gone Ole Miss's way: 52 wins against 49.6 deserved, 2.4 to the good, with a 15-7 record in one-score games and a turnover margin of +31. 2025 was the best of it (+1.6).

How sure is this?

One standard error on luck is about ±2.3 wins over five seasons, so +2.4 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.0 standard errors). Luck needs far more than 63 games to measure; anything under about 5 wins here cannot be told from nothing.

3. Was it the roster?

Three national rankings side by side: the roster's recruiting pedigree (247Sports talent composite), how well the team actually played (SP+), and where the preseason AP poll had it. Lower is better. When the play line sits below the talent line, the roster gave less than its rankings promised. Above it, more.

Talent compositeSP+ (quality of play)Preseason AP (blank = unranked)
SeasonTalentRecruiting classPreseason APSP+OffenseDefenseRecord
20212718–17173610-3
20222323211417448-5
202323232212142211-2
20242021627310-3
2025211621732013-2

Takeaway: Ole Miss has played above its roster: No. 10 in play against a No. 23 roster, 12 spots better than the recruiting rankings would predict, in 5 of 5 seasons. 2024 was the high point, a No. 20 roster that played like No. 2. The offense averaged No. 12 and the defense No. 25. The comparison that matters is the league: the average SEC gap is -11 spots, because the talent composite rates SEC rosters higher than they play, so by SEC standards this roster has overdelivered.

How sure is this?

Five seasons of rank averages carry roughly ±5 spots of noise; single-season gaps of 20 or more spots are well outside it. The league comparison is the fair one, since the talent composite is generous to every SEC roster.

4. Does it change as the season goes on?

Each faint line is one season, game by game: how many points Ole Miss beat expectations by, or fell short. The heavy line is the five-season average for that game of the year. The table pools the five seasons into early, middle, and late stretches. The expected margin already moves week to week as opinion changes, so a pattern here says the public was slow to adjust, in one direction or the other.

Part of seasonGamesWon-lostExpected winsAvg marginBeat by, avgPlay vs expected, per game
Early (games 1-4)2018-216.3+29.8+9.6+2%
Middle (5-8)2015-513.3+5.5-2.6+1%
Late (9 on)2719-817.2+8.6+0.2+8%

Takeaway: By margin, Ole Miss has faded as seasons go on: 0.2 points a game ahead of expectations from game 9 on, versus 9.6 points a game ahead of expectations in the first four. Because the expected margin already adjusts week by week, that means the public kept believing longer than the play warranted. In wins: 18-2 early against 16.3 expected (+1.7), 19-8 late against 17.2 expected (+1.8).

How sure is this?

One standard error on the early-versus-late margin difference is about ±4.4 points a game (20 early games, 27 late), so -9.4 is unlikely to be noise (2.1 standard errors). On the wins comparison one standard error is about ±2.6 wins, so +0.1 is within the noise (0.0 standard errors). Single-game swings of 20 points are routine, which is why the faint season lines look so jagged.

Bottom line: Expectations for Ole Miss have probably run too low (-2.7 wins, suggestive but not conclusive). It has probably been lucky (+2.4 wins, suggestive but not conclusive). The roster has outplayed its rankings by SEC standards (+12 spots against a league average of -11). Late-season form has been worse than early-season form by 9 points a game, and that is outside the noise.

Over five seasons Texas has been about what everyone expected: 48 wins against 48.6 expected. That does not mean nothing is going on underneath. Were the expectations right for the right reasons? Did the bounces even out? Did the roster play to its recruiting rankings? The sections below take those one at a time, then ask whether any of it changes as a season goes on. Each ends with a short takeaway; a note under it says how much to trust the number, because five seasons is only about 63 games.

Terms used on this page
Expected margin
How many points the team was expected to win or lose by, according to the point spread the sportsbooks posted just before kickoff. It sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public expected, with money behind it, so this page uses it as the measure of expectations. A week-earlier version (the opening number) also exists; when the two differ, opinion moved during the week.
Expected wins
Each game's expected margin converted to a chance of winning, then added up. The record the public thought was coming.
Deserved wins
Each game's postgame win probability, from CollegeFootballData's play-by-play model, added up. How many games a team that played that way usually wins. The gap between actual and deserved wins is what most people call luck.
SP+
Bill Connelly's efficiency rating of how well a team actually played, adjusted for opponent. Used here as the measure of quality, separate from the record.
Talent composite
247Sports' rating of the whole roster's recruiting pedigree. Used here as the measure of what the players were supposed to be.
Beat expectations (by)
Won by more than the expected margin, or lost by less. "Beat by" is the actual margin minus the expected margin: +7 means seven points better than expected. A bettor would say the team covered.
One-score game
Decided by eight points or fewer.
Standard error
The size of gap that random variation alone produces about a third of the time. A number within one standard error is noise. Beyond two, it is probably real. Each takeaway has a "How sure is this?" note that says which.

1. Were the expectations wrong?

Every game carries an expected margin, the point spread posted just before kickoff, which sums up what oddsmakers, bettors, and the public thought would happen. Convert each one to a chance of winning and add them up, and you get the record the public expected. Deserved wins come from the other direction: after each game, a play-by-play model estimates how often a team that played that way wins it. If the public expected more wins than the play deserved, the expectations were too optimistic.

The offense averaged No. 19 and the defense No. 26, so the defense has been the larger drag. The comparison that matters is the league: the average SEC gap is -11 spots, because the talent composite rates SEC rosters higher than they play, so against that baseline Texas is typical of the conference. Five seasons of rank averages carry roughly ±5 spots of noise; single-season gaps of 20 or more spots are well outside it. The league comparison is the fair one, since the talent composite is generous to every SEC roster.

Takeaway: By margin, Texas has faded as seasons go on: 0.1 points a game short of expectations from game 9 on, versus 5.7 points a game ahead of expectations in the first four. Because the expected margin already adjusts week by week, that means the public kept believing longer than the play warranted. In wins: 16-4 early against 15.8 expected (+0.2), 19-9 late against 18.4 expected (+0.6).

How sure is this?

One standard error on the early-versus-late margin difference is about ±4.4 points a game (20 early games, 28 late), so -5.8 is suggestive but not conclusive (1.3 standard errors). Single-game swings of 20 points are routine, which is why the faint season lines look so jagged.

Bottom line: Expectations for Texas have been about right (+1.3 wins, within the noise). Luck has been a non-factor (+0.8 wins, within the noise). The roster-to-play gap (-11 spots) is the SEC norm (-11); the talent rankings flatter the whole league, not just Texas.

Five seasons of rank averages carry roughly ±5 spots of noise; single-season gaps of 20 or more spots are well outside it. The league comparison is the fair one, since the talent composite is generous to every SEC roster.

4. Does it change as the season goes on?

Each faint line is one season, game by game: how many points Vanderbilt beat expectations by, or fell short. The heavy line is the five-season average for that game of the year. The table pools the five seasons into early, middle, and late stretches. The expected margin already moves week to week as opinion changes, so a pattern here says the public was slow to adjust, in one direction or the other.

Part of seasonGamesWon-lostExpected winsAvg marginBeat by, avgPlay vs expected, per game

Middle (5-8)207-135.4-12.6+0.5+2%

Takeaway: By margin, no real pattern: Vanderbilt was 3.8 points a game ahead of expectations early in seasons, 0.5 points a game ahead of expectations in the middle, and 2.5 points a game ahead of expectations late. In wins: 12-8 early against 11.3 expected (+0.7), 7-15 late against 5.9 expected (+1.1).

How sure is this?

One standard error on the early-versus-late margin difference is about ±4.6 points a game (20 early games, 22 late), so -1.3 is within the noise (0.3 standard errors). On the wins comparison one standard error is about ±2.5 wins, so +0.4 is within the noise (0.2 standard errors). Single-game swings of 20 points are routine, which is why the faint season lines look so jagged.

Bottom line: Expectations for Vanderbilt have been about right (-1.5 wins, within the noise). Luck has been a non-factor (+1.9 wins, within the noise). The roster has underdelivered even by SEC standards (-20 spots against a league average of -11).
